absent: Exact numeric values for low and high resolution granularity, tick period, hang delay bound and maximum time sentinel are not shown in these fragments.
Complete field order, sizes and padding for timer, CPU base, clock base, scheduler and tick device structures are not shown.
Selection conditions for alternate implementations such as high resolution disabled, low resolution time, verification builds and single-CPU builds are not shown.
Internals of referenced helpers for offset updates, hardware reprogramming, event programming, broadcast handling, timerfd notification and queue manipulation are not shown.
Lock ordering guarantees beyond the observed nesting of CPU reader, per-CPU base and expiry locks and preemption control are not shown.
CPU bring-up, hotplug migration, interrupt entry details and cross-CPU call delivery guarantees are not shown.

findings.text: Cancellation through the public interface settles through repeated underlying attempts, blocking only when the target is reported as running elsewhere, and finally reports whether the timer had been pending.

The start interface arms a timer for a deadline with a tolerance window and a mode selecting hardness and pinning. The caller observes only completion while any required update of the underlying event source is handled internally, including a forced path for contexts that cannot update locally.

The forward interface advances a deadline by whole multiples of a period relative to a supplied now and reports how many periods were missed. Very short periods are raised to the current timer granularity, and requests already in the future report no advance without modifying the timer.

The division helper converts a timestamp to scalar nanoseconds and divides by a signed divisor while preserving sign in the result. Wide divisors are reduced in magnitude with a compensating shift of the dividend so the final division fits the narrow operation.

The remaining-time query reports the interval until expiry for a timer, with an optional adjustment for coarse-grained configurations. The value is obtained under serialization that stabilizes concurrent arming and expiry.

The next-event queries report the earliest pending expiry on the local CPU, either overall or while ignoring one designated timer. When high resolution handling is active the overall query reports an unbounded value because comparison is delegated elsewhere, while the exclusion variant still considers hard and soft groups.

The wall-clock change notification refreshes per-CPU timer offsets and wakes only those CPUs whose earliest deadline moved earlier, falling back to waking all CPUs when temporary allocation fails. A deferred work variant allows the same notification from contexts that cannot perform the scan directly, and a timerfd notification always follows.

The one-shot transition requires a functional tick device with one-shot capability, installs a supplied handler and moves the device into one-shot state with broadcast coordination. Failures are reported after a diagnostic distinguishing missing, non-functional and incapable devices.

The scheduler-timer setup creates a per-CPU periodic timer for tick emulation, aligning its first expiry to the global jiffy phase with an optional per-CPU skew to reduce contention, arming it in a mode matching high-resolution availability and enabling nohz accounting.

Auxiliary interfaces allow updating a timer callback when the timer is idle, querying whether nohz mode is globally active, obtaining callback time for a timer clock identity, and deferring a nohz parameter refresh to workqueue context or to a no-op depending on configuration.

Each CPU maintains a collection of timer bases covering monotonic, realtime, boottime and TAI identities, each present in both a hard-expiry form and a soft-expiry form. A shared per-CPU lock and a cross-CPU notification block accompany the collection.

A dedicated standalone CPU base provides a parking location for timers detached from any online CPU. Its sole clock base refers back to its own container and carries a statically zeroed sequence counter tied to its lock.

High-resolution operation is governed by a boot-time flag defaulting to enabled and a runtime static branch initially disabled. The branch is enabled asynchronously through workqueue context after the underlying tick device has been switched, with empty variants eliminating the work when the feature is unavailable.

Debug tracking associates each timer with its callback for diagnostics and defines recovery for misuse. Initialization or release while active cancels the timer and completes the requested debug transition, activation while active is rejected with a diagnostic, and use without initialization installs a placeholder that warns and requests no restart.

Expiry selection across bases accounts for per-base time offsets and never reports a negative interval, clamping such results to zero. When one timer is excluded, selection substitutes the successor on any base where the excluded timer was earliest, leaving other bases unchanged.

The first jiffy phase is aligned upward to a whole tick multiple exactly once, with later callers observing the same stabilized value. The phase is protected so concurrent initializers serialize and readers observe a consistent value.

Nohz marking applies per scheduler state only when the global nohz feature is enabled, and the global refresh is triggered at most once across all CPUs. An alternate configuration removes both the marking and the refresh entirely.

Access to per-CPU timer bases and their queues requires holding the owning CPU base lock with interrupts contained. This covers scanning for the next event, arming, querying remaining or next expiry, updating callbacks under verification builds, and evaluating remote wake need during wall-clock changes. One next-event query may read a locally written active flag without the lock when interrupts are already disabled on the same CPU.

Global jiffy phase updates serialize writers with a dedicated lock while readers are protected by a sequence counter, and scheduler flag updates require interrupts to be disabled on the local CPU. Wall-clock propagation additionally holds the CPU reader lock across the online-CPU scan and contains preemption across the multicast wake.

Soft-expiry handling uses an additional expiry lock around queue processing, initialized once per CPU base and eliminated entirely in configurations without soft separation. When waiters are present, the holder temporarily releases both the CPU base lock and the expiry lock and reacquires them in the same order to allow progress.

The per-CPU timer container holds a serialization lock, an array of clock bases indexed by a small integer with an associated clock identity, and a cross-CPU callback block targeting the reprogramming routine. Runtime state observed alongside includes active-base mask, pending deadlines for hard and soft groups, deferral and hang indicators, and waiter counts.

The debug descriptor for timers carries a human-readable name and five handlers covering hint lookup plus recovery for initialization, activation, release, and use-before-initialization. The hint handler exposes the timer callback while the recovery handlers implement the lifecycle policy described separately.

The migration container mirrors the per-CPU layout but only index zero is initialized, with its back-pointer set to the container itself and its sequence state zeroed in association with the container lock. A shorthand alias refers directly to that sole initialized element.

A timer moves from queued to running during expiry, with the running slot set before removal and cleared after any restart decision, separated by ordering barriers so concurrent observers never see neither state. Restart requests requeue only when the callback did not already rearm the timer, and soft-queue processing additionally synchronizes with waiters.

The tick device transitions from its initial mode to one-shot exactly once after validation, installing the high-resolution handler and enabling broadcast coordination. The broadcast step has an empty variant where no coordination is required.

Arming distinguishes no update, local update and forced update outcomes. Rearming honors the chosen deadline while clearing deferral state, substituting a bounded delay from now when a hang was previously noted.

System entry for timer configuration includes a boot-time string parser that toggles high-resolution eligibility, a per-CPU scheduler-timer installer invoked during bring-up and mode switches, a soft-interrupt handler draining soft-expiry queues, and workqueue handlers for deferred high-resolution enabling and wall-clock propagation.

Misuse diagnostics include warnings for activating an already active debug-tracked timer, for invoking the placeholder callback, for forwarding or updating a queued timer, and for failing to enter high-resolution mode. Allocation failure during wall-clock propagation degrades to waking all CPUs rather than skipping updates, and detected hangs defer the next deadline by a bounded interval to avoid tight looping.

Arming reports one of three small codes for no action versus standard versus forced device update. Timer granularity starts at the low constant and moves to the high constant after a successful switch to high resolution handling.

The per-CPU collection contains eight bases, pairing four clock identities between hard and soft handling. Scheduler timing aligns to a fixed nanosecond tick period with an optional half-tick spread across CPUs, and unbounded queries use a maximum time sentinel.
